intro: A hands-on introduction to humanoid robotics—from motors and actuators to coordinated motion and learned behavior. Over four weeks, students work in teams to assemble, program, and test components of an open-source humanoid.
introSecondary: The hardware platform is based on Berkeley Humanoid Lite. Each week combines two lectures, a guided hardware lab, and a scaffolded Python assignment.

facts.label: Prerequisites
facts.value: Basic programming, such as an introductory computer science or robotics course or equivalent experience. Assignments use Python. No prior hardware assembly, control theory, or machine learning experience is required.

facts.label: Meeting times
facts.value: Lectures Tuesdays and Thursdays, 1:00–2:30 p.m.; hardware labs Fridays, 1:00–2:30 p.m.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: To be determined; separate lecture and lab spaces are planned

facts.label: Instructional hours
facts.value: 18 scheduled hours, plus one optional office hour each week

learn.text: How motors, transmissions, encoders, and feedback control combine to produce controlled joint motion. Students assemble and test an actuator module from prepared components and implement motor position control.

media.alt: Exploded render of the Berkeley Humanoid Lite 6512 cycloidal actuator: rear housing, dark motor shell, motor and input shafts, middle housing, output shaft halves, copper-colored cycloidal disk, and front housing laid out along the axis.
media.caption: Inside the actuator: an exploded render of the printed 6512 cycloidal module (BHL design, CC BY-SA 4.0).

learn.text: Robot modeling, forward and inverse kinematics, and trajectory generation. Teams assemble actuators into a limb, validate joint motion, and implement end-effector motion control in simulation.

media.alt: Render of a single Berkeley Humanoid Lite leg from hip actuators to flat foot.
media.caption: One leg of the Berkeley Humanoid Lite: five actuators from hip to ankle (render, CC BY-SA 4.0).

learn.text: Reinforcement learning for locomotion and the challenges of transferring policies from simulation to hardware. Teams integrate limbs into a lower-body assembly for supported tests and train a locomotion policy in a scaffolded simulation environment.

media.alt: Four simulated humanoid robots walking on a checkered floor in a two-by-two grid.
media.caption: The Week 3 scaffold: the same training pipeline walking four open robots in MuJoCo (simulation).

learn.text: Skill representations, sequencing, and integrated behavior. Teams complete system integration, implement a simple skill-sequencing task in simulation, and present a demonstration with a brief technical report.

media.alt: Front render of the complete Berkeley Humanoid Lite robot with legs, torso, and arms.
media.caption: The integrated humanoid: lower body, torso, and arms (render, CC BY-SA 4.0).

objectives: Explain how motors, transmissions, encoders, and feedback control produce controlled joint motion.
Model robot limbs and implement basic end-effector motion in simulation.
Train and evaluate a scaffolded locomotion policy and identify simulation-to-reality challenges.
Integrate and test robot subsystems, document results, and demonstrate coordinated behavior.

format.title: How the course works
paragraphs: Hardware components and software scaffolds are prepared in advance. Students work in teams on shared builds using prepared hardware kits, guided labs, and scaffolded Python exercises. Labs focus on assembly, wiring, testing, and integration rather than fabrication, which is what makes a 90-minute weekly lab feasible.

Activities include four weekly assignments, laboratory participation, and a final team demonstration and report. Instructors give feedback on understanding, testing, and documentation. No academic credit or formal grade is awarded.

outcomes.title: Outcomes and expectations
paragraphs: The course ends with a team demonstration and a brief technical report documenting hardware and software results.

Successful untethered walking and manipulation are stretch goals, not promised outcomes. Final demonstrations will reflect validated hardware capabilities. Simulation-based activities provide a parallel route for learning and evaluation whenever hardware needs troubleshooting.
Builds are shared team builds. Students do not each build, or take home, a complete robot.
